title: 3 Traits Of A Gifted Teacher
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Reflecting on a kindergarten lesson he watched delivered to a room of 50-plus observing adults, Linsin distills three traits that made the teacher instantly captivating. First, she was unapologetically herself, mismatched sweater and all, and that authenticity — rather than polish — is what held the room. Second, she was open to spontaneous humor, improvising off the energy in the room instead of relying on planned jokes or props. Third, she delivered one crystal-clear objective, using examples and comparisons until every listener, youngest to oldest, understood it completely. Linsin frames these as skills any teacher can access by staying present, being an expert in their content, and refusing to blur their lesson's purpose, arguing that clarity in particular has become a lost art in classrooms generally.
points: Authenticity outperforms polish: the closer a teacher stays to their true, unfiltered personality, the more compelling they become.
Humor works best when improvised in the moment rather than pre-planned, which requires being fully present and reading the room.
Clarity means having one specific, well-defined objective per lesson and using examples until it's understood by everyone in the room.
The teacher's power came from doing her job with no need for approval — she left without seeking praise or fanfare.
Most ineffective teaching stems from lessons without a clear singular purpose, leaving students confused about what's actually being asked of them.
quotes: It was clear to all watching, however, that she was completely at home in her own skin. What she presented, then, was her true personality.
The Lesson: The closer you are to your true personality, the more compelling a teacher you’ll be.
She was hilarious and spot on with her observations. She didn’t have planned jokes or stories. She didn’t use props or try to make anyone laugh.
Clear means crystalline, untainted, plain as day, and understood without question.
She took something complex and made it obvious and accessible. There was no doubt that everyone knew the objective forward and backward, including the youngest and the oldest in the room.
Everything you say and do must have a purpose. If it doesn’t move students closer to your objective, then you’re pushing them farther away. In the quest for effective teaching, clarity is king.
